newsitem.title: JORDAN: Jordan warns Israel against harsh security steps.
newsitem.headline: Jordan warns Israel against harsh security steps.

text.p: Jordan warned Israel on Saturday not to employ harsh security measures against Palestinians, saying a heavy hand in battling militants following bombings in Jerusalem would only backfire.

Acting Information Minister Nasser al-Lawzi said Jordan was worried Israel's security clampdown after suicide bombers killed 13 people in Jerusalem's main Jewish market on Wednesday was counterproductive and went beyond tackling its legitimate security concerns.

Lawzi told reporters after a cabinet meeting held to discuss the deteriorating situation that Foreign Minister Fayez al-Tarawanah had contacted Israeli and U.S. officials to urge Israel "not to overdo measures and employ toughness...in (Palestinian) self-rule areas".
"This will only lead to more tension and steering away from the main issue, which is security," Lawzi said.

Jordan is worried by the repercussions of renewed violence in Palestinian territories on its own stability. The kingdom's 4.2 million people have close ethnic ties with Palestinians in the West Bank and Gaza.

Officials also fear Israel's rightwing government, already deeply doubtful about peace accords signed by the previous Labour government, will use the Jerusalem attack as an excuse to further backtrack on its commitments to the Palestinians.
Jordan supports the Palestinian stance that Israel has been stalling on implementing a 1993 interim peace accord.

Lawzi also sharply criticised Israel's closure of the Palestinian territories which has confined its inhabitants to their home districts, saying it was a policy which could only result in more violence.

"Any closure that has taken place or will happen or existing now will only lead to more reactions...and will lead to more tension in the region and to more pressure," the minister added, saying the closures were unjustified and counterproductive.
Tarawnah also criticised Israel for its reaction to the bombing, saying it was critical that it perceived the Palestinian Authority as a partner and not an enemy.
"We say Israel has to consider the Palestinian Authority as a partner and not as an enemy or adversary and the security issue has to be viewed within that perspective," Tarawnah told reporters.

While Jordan respected Israeli security concerns, the Jewish state should not allow the bombing to force it to retreat on progress far attained in interim peace accords with the Palestinians, Tarawnah added.

King Hussein has expressed increasing exasperation with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's policies, publicly doubting his resolve to advance the peace process and warning about the dangers of an accelerated Jewish settlement drive in the West Bank.
